title: Greedy Best-First on Lisbon: Fast, But Can Mislead ⚡
description: Watch Greedy Best-First Search race toward the destination using only a heuristic—then fail when “closest-looking” streets trap it. This reel visualizes the exact greedy vs A* tradeoff for heuristic pathfinding.
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — why Greedy rushes ⚡
In Lisbon (Alfama), Greedy Best-First always picks the next node with the smallest heuristic h(n) (usually straight-line distance to the goal). That means it ignores the cost-so-far g(n), so the frontier can look “promising” while silently walking into dead ends or long backtracks.

✅ How to read the animation: the algorithm’s priority queue is ordered only by h(n), so the path “snaps” toward the target’s direction.

⚠️ When it fails: with misleading heuristics (or obstacles that force detours), Greedy can commit early and produce a suboptimal path—while A* balances g(n)+h(n) to recover.

Takeaway: Greedy Best-First is fast and goal-focused, but it’s not guaranteed to find the shortest route.

Question for you: Would you rather always be fast-to-goal (Greedy) or guaranteed-shortest (A*)?

In this Lisbon (Alfama) visualization, you’ll see how Greedy Best-First expands nodes using only the heuristic h(n) (goal distance), skipping the cost-so-far g(n). That single design choice can create confident-looking paths that become inefficient or get stuck—while A* uses g(n)+h(n) to improve optimality.
